title: Judge People by Their Character, Not Their Labels
excerpt: It's easy to judge people by their views, beliefs or the groups they belong to. But these labels rarely tell the whole story. Real character is revealed through kindness, empathy and how we treat others. Before deciding who someone is, give them the chance to show you.
content:
It's surprisingly easy to form an opinion about someone before we've even met them. We see something they've posted online, hear which political party they support, learn about their beliefs or find out they belong to a particular group, and almost straight away we start making assumptions about what kind of person they are.

Sometimes those assumptions come from our own experiences. Other times they're shaped by what we've heard from friends, the media or people we trust. Before we've had a proper conversation with someone, we may already have decided whether we'd like them, whether we'd get along, or whether we want them in our lives.

How fair is that? And how many good relationships do we miss because we judged someone before giving them a chance?

I believe we should judge people by their character, not by the labels they carry or the opinions they hold. The only way to really understand someone's character is to spend time with them and see how they behave.

## You don't know someone until you know them

We all have our own beliefs, values and opinions, shaped by our upbringing, experiences, relationships and the places we grew up. Even two people in similar circumstances can reach very different conclusions.

Political views are a good example. Two people might support different parties or disagree strongly about how to handle a particular issue. It's easy to assume those differences tell you everything you need to know about each other, but they rarely do. One person may have reached their position through their own experiences, and another may have reached a different one through experiences of their own. They can disagree about the solution to a problem while both believing they're trying to do the right thing.

Some views deserve serious scrutiny, and I'll come back to that. But challenging an opinion is different from deciding you already understand the whole character of the person who holds it. If we dismiss someone before we've spoken to them, we lose the chance to find out who they are.

## Character is revealed through how we treat people

For me, the qualities that say most about a person are things like kindness, empathy, honesty and respect. How do they treat people? Will they listen to a different perspective? Do they show compassion when someone is struggling? Can they admit when they're wrong?

I also pay attention to how people treat those who have nothing to offer them. It's easy to be pleasant to someone who can help your career, give you something you want or improve your social standing. You learn far more by watching how someone behaves towards a stranger, a service worker, or anyone who can't do anything for them in return.

Those everyday moments reveal a lot, and so does the way someone behaves when they're frustrated, challenged or under pressure. Anyone can talk about being a good person. Behaviour is what gives the words meaning.

None of us gets everything right, of course. We all have bad days, make mistakes and sometimes behave in ways we regret. Judging character means looking at the bigger picture and the patterns in someone's behaviour, and being willing to see both their strengths and their shortcomings. It doesn't mean expecting perfection.

## Disagreement doesn't have to mean division

It can be tempting to treat disagreement as a reason to keep our distance. We surround ourselves with people who share our views and grow more suspicious of those who don't.

Social media can make this worse. We often see the most extreme, provocative versions of other people's opinions instead of having ordinary conversations with individuals who believe different things. It becomes easy to see people as representatives of a group, and to forget they have their own experiences, relationships, worries and ambitions.

Imagine how limited life would be if we could only build relationships with people who agreed with us about everything.

You don't have to change your beliefs to get to know someone, and you don't have to pretend to agree with them either. You can disagree, explain your perspective, listen to theirs, and still recognise the qualities you value in each other.

Being able to disagree respectfully is an important part of healthy relationships. It means listening, managing your own reactions and accepting that someone can see the world differently without every conversation becoming a battle over who's right. Sometimes those conversations will challenge our assumptions. Sometimes we'll understand where the other person is coming from without changing our minds at all. Both are worthwhile.

## Being open-minded doesn't mean having no standards

Judging people by their character doesn't mean overlooking harmful behaviour or accepting everything someone says and does.

If someone repeatedly treats others with cruelty, ignores boundaries or uses their beliefs to justify mistreating people, that matters. We shouldn't excuse it because they're pleasant to us personally or because we share other interests.

Being open-minded means trying to understand people before reaching conclusions, while keeping your own values and paying attention to what you discover along the way. You can listen to someone's experiences, try to understand their perspective, and still decide that certain behaviour is unacceptable. What matters is basing that judgement on something more substantial than a label, a rumour or an assumption about what someone must be like.

## Give people a chance to surprise you

Some of the most interesting people we meet are the ones we first assumed we had little in common with. Once we get past the obvious differences, we might find shared values, a similar sense of humour, or experiences that help us understand each other. We might also find our first impressions were completely wrong.

That won't happen every time. Sometimes getting to know someone will confirm our concerns, and that's fine. Nobody has to like everyone or befriend people whose values clash with their own. The aim is to make a better-informed judgement.

I think there's a lot to be said for approaching people with curiosity instead of suspicion. Instead of immediately asking whether someone fits our idea of a good person, we can listen, ask questions and watch how they behave. We might learn something about them, or about ourselves, and occasionally we might rethink an assumption we've held for years.

## Judge the person, not the label

We all want to be seen as individuals. Most of us would like others to look past our mistakes, understand our intentions and recognise that we're more complicated than a single opinion or decision. Yet it's easy to forget to offer other people the same courtesy.

We can disagree with someone's politics, question their opinions and challenge their decisions without reducing them to those things. We can recognise kindness in someone whose views differ from ours, just as we should be willing to recognise poor character in someone who shares our beliefs.

So before deciding what kind of person someone is, give yourself the chance to meet them. Have the conversation, listen to what they say and pay attention to what they do. You don't have to agree with everyone, like everyone or invite everyone into your life, but you can give people a fair chance to show you who they are.
